scenes.tts: The first film followed D N A changes through one expanding lineage. How can mixed D N A reads reveal which tumor lineage carries a change? Start with that same clay-colored family tree. An early clay marker appears near its trunk. Every later branch inherits it.

scenes.visual: Reuse the first film's COLOR MAP: pale grey ordinary cells and DNA; clay orange somatic change; gold germline; green working suppressor; red lost function; teal reads. Blue is not used in this film. Fill the frame with the same clay family tree growing from one cell. Add one filled clay circle badge at the trunk; duplicate it into every descendant as branches grow.
scenes.narration: The first film followed DNA changes through one expanding lineage. How can mixed DNA reads reveal which tumor lineage carries a change? Start with that same clay-colored family tree. An early clay marker appears near its trunk. Every later branch inherits it.

scenes.visual: Transform the branching tree into the title 'Reading a Tumor Family Tree' for two seconds. Branch tips continue drifting behind it.

scenes.tts: Later, one branch gains a second, square marker. Only that branch carries it, so it is a subclone. The trunk marker is clonal because every tumor branch carries it. The pattern records ancestry, even when the sample mixes all branches together.

scenes.visual: Carry the tree. Add a small clay-outlined square to one late branch and copy it only through that branch. Enclose all branch tips in a sample tube while keeping faint lines back to the tree. Label the filled clay circle 'clonal' and the late square 'subclonal' only after their distributions are visible.

scenes.tts: Now place a matched-normal sample beside the tumor. It comes from the same person, often from blood. A variant found only in tumor is usually somatic. A variant found in both samples is usually germline, most often inherited. The word usually matters.

scenes.visual: Split the mixed sample into two large tubes labelled 'tumor' and 'matched normal'. Teal read tiles flow upward from each. A clay variant tile appears only in tumor. A gold variant tile appears in both. Attach the word 'usually' to both interpretations. Keep at most six read tiles visible per tube.
scenes.narration: Now place a matched-normal sample beside the tumor. It comes from the same person, often from blood. A variant found only in tumor is usually somatic. A variant found in both samples is usually germline, most often inherited. The word usually matters.

scenes.tts: Here is a gold variant in both tumor and matched normal. Predict: did it most likely enter this person's cells before the tumor lineage began, or after one tumor branch formed?
scenes.caption: Here is a gold variant in both tumor and matched normal. Predict: did it most likely enter this person's cells before the tumor lineage began, or after one tumor branch formed?
scenes.visual: Keep both tubes large. Highlight the same gold rectangular variant among teal reads in both. Draw two neutral timeline slots below: 'before tumor lineage' and 'after one tumor branch'. Do not highlight either answer. Read tiles drift slowly.
scenes.narration: Here is a gold variant in both tumor and matched normal. Predict: did it most likely enter this person's cells before the tumor lineage began, or after one tumor branch formed?

scenes.visual: Hold the question and two neutral timeline slots. Keep teal read tiles moving gently through both tubes.

scenes.tts: Most likely, it was present before the tumor lineage began. So it is usually germline, whether inherited or newly formed in an egg or sperm. The matched normal gives the timing clue. Tumor data alone cannot reliably separate that history from a somatic change.

scenes.visual: Highlight 'before tumor lineage' in gold. Move the gold badge to the root before the clay tumor tree starts, then copy it into pale normal cells and every tumor branch. Collapse the matched-normal tube briefly; replace the timing answer with a question mark until the tube returns.

scenes.tts: Variant allele fraction, or V A F, is the fraction of reads carrying a variant. A clonal variant can still sit below one half. Normal cells dilute the tumor reads. Copy gains, losses, and loss of heterozygosity also change the number of variant and nonvariant copies.
scenes.caption: Variant allele fraction, or VAF, is the fraction of reads carrying a variant. A clonal variant can still sit below one half. Normal cells dilute the tumor reads. Copy gains, losses, and loss of heterozygosity also change the number of variant and nonvariant copies.
scenes.visual: Transform the tubes into a large teal read counter: variant tiles move to the numerator lane and all tiles to the denominator lane. Mix pale normal-cell tiles into clay tumor-cell tiles, visibly lowering the variant share. Then duplicate and remove labelled rectangular copy blocks. Mark all counts 'schematic'; do not show a molecular structure.
scenes.narration: Variant allele fraction, or VAF, is the fraction of reads carrying a variant. A clonal variant can still sit below one half. Normal cells dilute the tumor reads. Copy gains, losses, and loss of heterozygosity also change the number of variant and nonvariant copies.

scenes.tts: Purity is the fraction of cells in the sample that are tumor cells. For a heterozygous clonal variant in a two-copy region, expected V A F is purity times one half. The shortcut also assumes normal cells lack the variant. It fails after copy changes or loss of the other allele, or when only a subclone carries it.
scenes.caption: Purity is the fraction of cells in the sample that are tumor cells. For a heterozygous clonal variant in a two-copy region, expected VAF is purity times one half. scenes.visual: Show a large sample box whose clay tumor-cell share grows while pale normal cells shrink. Beside it, build the text relation 'expected VAF = purity × 0.5' from labelled blocks, not spoken digits. Then branch the relation toward four warning icons: 'normal cells carry it', 'copy number changed', 'other allele lost' and 'subclone'. Keep labels high contrast.

scenes.tts: So read the evidence in order. Compare tumor with matched normal. Ask which lineages carry the variant. Then count mutant copies against all copies. Purity, copy number, and read depth limit the inference. The result is a family-tree estimate, not a perfect replay.

scenes.visual: Rebuild the carried tree on the left and the two sample tubes on the right. Animate three arrows in order: compare samples, map the variant to branches, count copies. Add small boundary labels 'purity', 'copy number', and 'read depth' around a dashed estimate frame. Keep every branch visible but moving slowly.
scenes.narration: So read the evidence in order. Compare tumor with matched normal. Ask which lineages carry the variant. Then count mutant copies against all copies. Purity, copy number, and read depth limit the inference. The result is a family-tree estimate, not a perfect replay.

scenes.tts: A high or low fraction is not a verdict by itself. Read it with the matched normal and the sample's copy structure. Different branch histories can produce similar fractions, so the supporting clues matter. That uncertainty belongs in the interpretation. Together, those clues connect mixed sequencing reads back to the expanding cell lineages that produced them.
